progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c03 (intramolecular against intermolecular; dispersion forces from temporary dipoles; more electrons and more contact give stronger dispersion forces; branching lowers boiling point, "spaghetti and balls"; water's hydrogen bonds and why hexane forms a layer; "like dissolves like"; tetrahedral carbons), chem-m7-c01 and g01 (naming rules: longest chain, nearer end, locants, methyl and ethyl branches, the multiple bond wins the numbering), chem-m7-c02 ("-ol means an O–H group, the number says which carbon"; propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol as position isomers; ethanol), chem-m7-c04a (ethanol from ethene and steam; propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol named as possible products). Year 11: electronegativity and polar bonds; lone pairs; hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular force between H on N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F. Not assumed: alcohol, hydroxyl group, primary, secondary, tertiary, donor, acceptor.
progression.startsWith: Identify the OH group and classify its carbon. The video opens: The gas in this camping stove is mostly butane, which boils near minus one degree. The liquid in this bottle is ethanol. Ethanol molecules have fewer electrons than butane, so you'd expect weaker dispersion forces and a lower boiling point.
progression.stopsAfter: identifying the OH group and its polar bond; naming alcohols up to C8 with methyl or ethyl branches; classifying alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary; explaining why an alcohol boils higher than an alkane of the same size; explaining the boiling point trend along the series and across C₄H₁₀O isomers; explaining why short-chain alcohols mix with water and longer ones barely dissolve. No reactions, no production, no combustion data.
progression.nextLesson: making ethanol by hydration, haloalkane substitution and fermentation (route chem-m7-c06, "How can we make ethanol?").

teaching.task: An ethanol molecule has fewer electrons than butane, yet ethanol boils about eighty degrees higher and mixes with water. How does one OH group change an alcohol's properties, and how do we name and classify alcohols?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) ethanol has fewer electrons than butane yet boils higher and mixes with water (1); (2) an alcohol is an alkane with one H swapped for a covalent OH; oxygen pulls the shared electrons, so the O–H bond is polar, and O keeps two lone pairs (2); (3) the name locates the OH: "-ol" with the locant from the nearer end (3); (4) the OH wins the numbering over a branch, because it is in the ending (4); (5) count the carbons on the C–OH carbon to classify (5); (6) branching elsewhere does not change the class (6); (7) the δ+ H of one molecule is attracted to a lone pair on a neighbour's O: a hydrogen bond, added to the chain's dispersion forces (7); (8) with equal electrons, the alcohol boils far higher, because of the hydrogen bonds; boiling breaks no covalent bond (8); (9) along the series the OH is constant, the chain grows, so dispersion forces and boiling points rise (9); (10) for isomers, compact shapes touch less, so weaker dispersion forces and lower boiling points; all still hydrogen bond (10); (11) the OH hydrogen bonds with water, replacing what it breaks, so small alcohols mix (11); (12) the chain breaks water's hydrogen bonds without replacing them, so solubility falls as it grows; long chains suit non-polar solvents (12); memory aid (13); two attempts and brief feedback (14 to 17); handoff (18); key notes (19).
teaching.conversationalApproach: ethanol has fewer electrons than butane yet boils about eighty degrees higher and mixes with water, so the video asks how one OH group changes a molecule's properties and how alcohols are named and classified. The hydroxyl group is introduced on a carbon with only single bonds, covalent and not a hydroxide ion, with a polar O-H bond and two lone pairs on the oxygen. Naming drops the alkane's final e and adds ol with the OH carbon's number, and the OH wins the numbering over a branch. Class comes from counting the carbons bonded to the OH carbon (primary, secondary, tertiary, methanol by convention), never from how branched a molecule looks. Hydrogen bonds form between a hydrogen of one OH and a lone pair on a neighbour's oxygen, so propane and ethanol, with the same electrons, boil about 120 degrees apart. Along the series the chain sets the trend because each alcohol has one OH; among isomers the compact tertiary one touches less and boils lowest, so shape does the work. Small alcohols mix with water because the OH replaces the hydrogen bonds it breaks, while a longer chain breaks more than it can replace and dissolves less. The memory aid is same size, hydrogen bonding wins; same family, size wins. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: The gas in this camping stove is mostly butane, which boils near minus one degree. The liquid in this bottle is ethanol. Ethanol molecules have fewer electrons than butane, so you'd expect weaker dispersion forces and a lower boiling point. Instead, ethanol boils at about seventy eight degrees. And it mixes completely with water, while butane barely dissolves. The difference is one O H group. So how does an O H group change a molecule's properties?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "An alcohol has the condensed structural formula CH₃CH(OH)CH(CH₃)CH₃. Give its IUPAC name, and classify it as a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol. Justify your classification." A skeletal formula is shown beside it (plain ink, no colours). New molecule (scenes use 4-methylpentan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol); tests the OH winning the numbering and the carbon count. Crossed mistake: "2-methylbutan-3-ol" (numbered for the branch; the c01 feedback 1 pattern). (A2) "Butane, C₄H₁₀, boils at −1 °C. Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, boils at 97 °C. Both molecules have 34 electrons. Explain the difference in boiling points, with reference to the intramolecular and intermolecular bonding present." New pair (the scene uses propane and ethanol); the syllabus wording. Crossed mistake: "Propan-1-ol is polar, so it has a higher boiling point." (names no force; the marker-reported mistake in 2020 Q32, `../research/question-types-chem-m7.md`).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "investigate the nomenclature of organic chemicals, up to C8, using IUPAC conventions, including simple methyl and ethyl branched chains, including: (ACSCH127); alkanes; alkenes; alkynes; alcohols (primary, secondary and tertiary); aldehydes and ketones; carboxylic acids; amines and amides; halogenated organic compounds" This video covers alcohols only (hydrocarbons were chem-m7-c01 and g01; haloalkanes chem-m7-c04a). "investigate the structural formulae, properties and functional group including:; primary; secondary; tertiary alcohols" "explain the properties within and between the homologous series of alcohols with reference to the intermolecular and intramolecular bonding present" this video starts by identifying the OH group and classifying the carbon that holds it, and stops at explaining the boiling point and solubility trends of alcohols. It teaches: an alcohol has an OH (hydroxyl) group on a carbon with only single bonds; the OH is covalently bonded, not a hydroxide ion (spoken), so alcohols do not make water alkaline (screen line only); intramolecular bonding: the O–H bond (and the C–O bond) is polar because oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly, so O is δ− and H is δ+, and the oxygen keeps two lone pairs; naming alcohols by IUPAC rules (longest chain containing the C–OH carbon; drop the alkane's final "e" and add "ol"; number from the end nearer the OH; locant before "ol"; methanol and ethanol need no locant; branches as in c01; the OH wins the numbering over a branch); classification by counting the carbons bonded to the C–OH carbon (1 primary, 2 secondary, 3 tertiary; methanol counted as primary by convention; branching elsewhere does not change the class); hydrogen bonding between alcohol molecules (δ+ H of one OH to a lone pair on a neighbour's O; H donor, O acceptor), alongside dispersion forces from the chain; between series: an alcohol boils far higher than an alkane with the same number of electrons (propane and ethanol, 26 electrons each), and boiling overcomes the intermolecular forces without breaking the O–H bond; within the series: one OH each, so similar hydrogen bonding, and boiling point rises with chain length (methanol to butan-1-ol); isomers of C₄H₁₀O: boiling point usually falls from primary to secondary to tertiary because the more compact shape gives less contact and weaker dispersion forces, while all three hydrogen bond; solubility: the OH hydrogen bonds with water, replacing the bonds it breaks, so methanol to propan-1-ol mix in any proportion; the non-polar chain breaks water's hydrogen bonds without replacing them, so solubility falls gradually with chain length (butan-1-ol partly, hexan-1-ol barely, as a layer); long-chain alcohols mix with non-polar solvents. Not here: alcohol reactions (combustion chem-m7-c07; dehydration, substitution with HX and oxidation chem-m7-c08; the class is used there, so one forward clause only); producing alcohols (chem-m7-c06, the next video); enthalpy of combustion (chem-m7-c07, p03, g02; the site's L11 figures are not used); methanol's toxicity (site hook; it is metabolic, not an intermolecular-force property, see Decisions); diols and alcohols with a C=C (not needed up to this route stop; author note e); branching and water solubility (2-methylpropan-2-ol; author note d; key notes leave it out); comparison with carboxylic acids, aldehydes and ketones (chem-m7-c08b, c09); hydrogen bond energies as numbers.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m7-c01 to c04b: carbon skeleton ink; hydrogens soft grey; main chain pale blue; branches amber; oxygen brick red, the OH group ringed red as the functional group; δ− and δ+ small in navy; lone pairs as two small red dot pairs on O; hydrogen bonds dotted violet; dispersion forces dotted pale blue. Board layout (constant): top-left the short task chip ("Name it", "Classify it", "Why higher?"); centre the structure board or force view, one molecule or one comparison at a time; the boiling point strip at the right only in scenes 8 to 10; plates small at the left or right only in scenes 1, 8, 12 and 18. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends; the previous case leaves before the next one draws. Reuse: painted plates (inspected 22 Oct): `m7-camping-gas-burner-v1.png` (a lit blue camping stove on an unlabelled blue gas canister; 2000 × 2000; hook and scene 8 callback, as in c01 and c03) and `m7-ethanol-fuel-bottle-v1.png` (an amber glass bottle with a glass stopper, about two-thirds full of a pale liquid, no label or text; 2000 × 2000; hook and handoff, with a coded label "ethanol"). Both small, scale uniformly only, never stretched. Considered, not used: `m6-red-wine-glass-v1.png` (inspected: a red wine glass; a drink would raise alcohol-consumption context the question does not need), `m7-crude-oil-barrel-v1.png` (inspected: plain steel drum; belongs to production in c06). New plate: `m7-alcohol-water-tubes-v1.png` (scene 12); see Assets. No human figures.
